summary: Question claims, weigh evidence and reach conclusions you can defend.
goals: Separate facts, opinions and assumptions in a statement
Test a claim using the QEAC checklist: Question, Evidence, Alternatives, Conclusion
Spot common reasoning traps such as bandwagon and false either-or
idea: Critical thinking is the habit of asking, 'How do I know this is true?' before believing or sharing something. It does not mean criticising everything; it means weighing evidence fairly and being willing to change your mind. In a world of viral posts, forwarded messages and persuasive adverts, it is a survival skill.

A claim is stronger when it comes from a reliable source, is supported by several independent pieces of evidence and still holds up when you consider other explanations. Our brains also take shortcuts, such as believing what most people believe or what fits what we already think. Knowing these traps helps us avoid them.
oneLine: Before you believe or share a claim, question it, check the evidence and consider alternatives.
steps: Question: what exactly is being claimed, who is saying it and why?
Evidence: what proof is given, is it reliable and can it be checked in at least two independent sources?
Alternatives: what other explanations could fit the facts, and who disagrees and why?
Conclusion: decide how confident you are (certain, probably, unsure) and say what would change your mind
scenarioSetup: A WhatsApp broadcast says, 'Drinking hot water with lemon cures all infections. Forward to 10 people to save lives.' It has a photo of a person in a white coat.
scenarioWrong: Amaka forwards it to 15 contacts because it sounds helpful and many people have shared it.
scenarioBetter: Question: who wrote it and what is the exact claim: 'cures all infections'?
Evidence: she finds no named source; she searches the World Health Organization and a health ministry site and finds nothing supporting it
Alternatives: lemon water may be healthy, but it does not cure infections
Conclusion: 'Almost certainly false.' She replies to the sender with the checked facts and does not forward it.
mistakes: Mistake: trusting a claim because many people share it. Fix: Popularity is not proof.
Mistake: only looking for evidence that agrees with you. Fix: Search for the best argument against your view.
Mistake: treating all sources as equal. Fix: Ask who benefits and who checked it.
lab: (5 min) Sort ten statements into fact, opinion or assumption
(10 min) Take one viral claim and run the QEAC checklist in groups
(10 min) Find two independent sources for or against it
(5 min) Each group states its confidence level and what would change its mind
reflect: What have I believed or shared that turned out to be false?
Which of my opinions have I never questioned?
Whose views do I rarely listen to, and why?
takeaways: Check claims before believing or sharing
Look for the best opposing argument
Confidence should match the strength of evidence
challenge: Choose a claim you saw this week (news, social media or advert) and test it with QEAC in writing. Share your verdict with a friend or family member and add your analysis to your portfolio.

check.q: What is the best first step when you see a surprising claim online?
o: Ask who says it and what evidence supports it
Believe it if many people share it
Because the first explanation may not be the only or best one
So you never reach a conclusion
A named expert or organisation with checkable evidence

summary: Generate many ideas, then choose and improve the best using divergent and convergent thinking.
goals: Explain divergent and convergent thinking and when to use each
Use SCAMPER prompts to improve an existing product or idea
Defer judgement during brainstorming to produce more ideas
idea: Creativity is not a gift only artists have; it is the ability to produce ideas that are both new and useful, and it can be practised. Creative thinking has two phases. Divergent thinking is going wide: producing as many ideas as possible without judging. Convergent thinking is narrowing: choosing, combining and improving the best ones.

Most people mix the two phases and kill ideas too early by saying, 'That will never work.' Teams that separate them, first a burst of quantity, then selection, produce better results. Prompts like SCAMPER give your brain handles to hold, so you are not staring at a blank page.
oneLine: Go wide first (no judging), then narrow down and improve.
steps: Substitute and Combine: what could you replace, or what could you join with something else?
Adapt and Modify: what could you copy from another field, or make bigger, smaller or different?
Put to another use and Eliminate: who else could use this, and what could you remove?
Reverse or Rearrange: what if the order, role or direction were flipped? Then converge: pick the three best ideas and test them
scenarioSetup: A school wants to reduce the plastic bottles littering its field. The student council brainstorms, but the first person says, 'Just ban bottles,' and the others agree because no one wants to argue.
scenarioWrong: Only one idea is explored, it is not popular, and the plastic keeps piling up.
scenarioBetter: Diverge: 30 ideas in 10 minutes without comment
Substitute: refill stations instead of bottles
Combine: a reward app that pays points for refills
Reverse: 'bottle bank' collection and recycling art
Converge: vote on three, prototype the refill station and test for a month.
mistakes: Mistake: judging ideas while generating them. Fix: Use 'Yes, and...' during the wide phase.
Mistake: stopping at the first good idea. Fix: Aim for quantity; the best idea is often the 15th.
Mistake: only brainstorming alone. Fix: Mix solo thinking with group sharing.
lab: (5 min) Pick an everyday object, such as a school bag
(10 min) Generate 20 SCAMPER improvements in pairs
(5 min) Converge: choose three and combine them
(10 min) Sketch and pitch the best idea in 60 seconds
reflect: When do my best ideas come to me?
What do I say that kills ideas, mine or others'?
What problem at school or home needs a creative fix?
challenge: Choose a real problem and produce 30 ideas using SCAMPER over three days, then pick and improve the best one. Add your idea list and the chosen idea sketch to your portfolio; it can seed your Quarter 3 Capstone.

o: Producing many ideas without judging them

check.q: Why separate brainstorming from selecting ideas?
o: Early judging kills ideas before they develop

check.q: Which SCAMPER prompt asks you to change the order or direction?

summary: Find the real cause of a problem and test small solutions before committing.
goals: Define a problem clearly before looking for solutions
Use the 5 Whys to move from symptom to root cause
Test a solution on a small scale and learn from the results
idea: Problem solving is more than finding answers; it starts with asking the right question. Many solutions fail because they fix the symptom, not the cause. If you keep mopping up a leaking roof without finding the hole, you will mop forever.

Good problem solvers work in loops: define the problem precisely, dig for root causes, generate options, try a small test, and learn from what happens. Small experiments are cheaper and safer than big bets, and they turn a scary problem into a series of learnable steps.
oneLine: Define it, dig to the root cause, test small, then scale what works.
steps: Define: write the problem in one sentence with who, what and how you know, such as '40% of Year 9 students submit homework late'
Dig: ask 'Why?' up to five times until you reach a cause you can act on
Design: list at least three possible solutions and pick one to test
Test: try it small for a short time, measure the result and adjust
scenarioSetup: A community group notices that the local borehole keeps running dry. They plan to ask for a second borehole.
scenarioWrong: They spend months raising funds for a new borehole, which runs dry too, because the real cause was never found.
scenarioBetter: Define: 'The borehole runs dry by 10 am daily for the past month'
Dig: Why? Pump runs all day. Why? Tank leaks. Why? A cracked pipe. Why not fixed? No one is responsible for maintenance
Design: three options: repair the pipe, appoint a caretaker, install a timer
Test: repair the pipe, appoint a caretaker and measure water levels for two weeks.
mistakes: Mistake: jumping to solutions. Fix: Spend time defining the problem.
Mistake: blaming people instead of processes. Fix: Ask what in the system allowed this.
Mistake: launching a big solution untested. Fix: Pilot with a small group first.
lab: (5 min) Choose a real school or community problem
(10 min) Write a clear problem statement and do a 5 Whys chain
(10 min) Brainstorm three solutions and design a small test with a measure
(5 min) Present your chain to another group for challenge
reflect: What problem do I keep 'solving' without success?
Who could help me see the root cause?
What small experiment can I run this week?
takeaways: A well-defined problem is half solved
challenge: Pick a real problem (family, school or community), run a 5 Whys analysis and test one small solution for one week, recording the result. Add your analysis and test results to your portfolio.

check.q: What is the aim of the 5 Whys?
o: To move from a symptom to a root cause

check.q: Why test a solution on a small scale first?
o: It is cheaper and safer, and it gives you data
40% of Year 9 students submit homework late this term

summary: Make better decisions with clear options, criteria and a check for regret and risk.
goals: Use a decision matrix to compare options against weighted criteria
Tell reversible from irreversible decisions and set the right effort level
Apply the 10-10-10 test to reduce emotional decision-making
idea: Every day you make decisions, from small ones like what to eat to big ones such as choosing subjects. Good decisions are not always good outcomes; they are choices made with the best information and reasoning you had. Decisions go wrong when we rush, follow the crowd or ignore what matters to us.

A simple structure helps: list real options, decide what criteria matter most, score each option and check the result against your gut feeling. Also ask whether a decision is reversible. A reversible decision, like trying a club, can be made quickly. An irreversible one, like leaving school, deserves much more care and advice.
oneLine: List options, weigh what matters, test the result, and spend more time on decisions you cannot undo.
steps: Options: list at least three real options, including 'do nothing' and a creative option
Criteria: choose four to five things that matter (cost, interest, future use, effect on family) and weight each from 1 to 5
Weigh: score each option on each criterion, multiply by the weight and add up the totals
Test: ask the 10-10-10 question: how will I feel about this in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years? Then decide and set a date to review
scenarioSetup: Bayo must choose between Physics, Economics and Art as his optional subject. His friends are choosing Economics, and his uncle says, 'Take Physics, it is serious.'
scenarioWrong: He picks Economics because friends are there, then struggles because he does not enjoy numbers and it does not match his goal of designing buildings.
scenarioBetter: Options: Physics, Economics, Art, and 'trial two lessons of each'
Criteria: interest (weight 5), link to architecture (5), difficulty (3), friends (1)
Weigh: Art and Physics score highest; Economics scores low
Test: 10-10-10 shows he would regret not choosing a subject linked to his dream. He picks Physics and keeps drawing as a club.
mistakes: Mistake: deciding only when emotional. Fix: Sleep on it when possible.
Mistake: considering only two options. Fix: Add a third, creative option.
Mistake: treating all decisions as life-or-death. Fix: Decide quickly on reversible choices.
lab: (5 min) Write a real decision you face
(10 min) Build a decision matrix with four criteria and weights
(10 min) Run the 10-10-10 test and compare it with the matrix result
(5 min) Discuss with a partner what the matrix revealed
reflect: What was my best decision and what made it good?
Do I decide mostly on feelings, friends or facts?
Which pending decision needs more information?
takeaways: Weights show what really matters to you
Reversible choices deserve speed, irreversible ones deserve care
challenge: Use a decision matrix on one real decision this week and record the final choice and your reasons. In two weeks, review how it turned out. Add the matrix and review to your portfolio.

check.q: What is a decision matrix used for?
Which decision most deserves long, careful thought?
o: An irreversible choice like leaving school
How will I feel in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years?

summary: Reason through ethical dilemmas and build a personal ethical standard you can explain.
goals: Identify who is affected by each option in a dilemma
Use three tests: Who is affected? What if everyone did this? Could I explain it to someone I respect?
Explain the difference between ethics and simply following rules
idea: Ethics is about deciding what is fair and right using consistent principles, not just following what is comfortable or what the loudest person suggests. Real dilemmas are rarely 'right versus wrong'; they are often 'right versus right', where two things you value pull in different directions.

There is not always one agreed 'correct' answer to an ethical problem, but there is better and worse reasoning. Good reasoning considers everyone affected, tests the choice against fairness ('what if everyone did this?') and is honest enough to be explained in public. Ethical courage means holding the standard when it is inconvenient or costly.
oneLine: Weigh who is affected, test the choice as a universal rule, and be ready to explain it openly.
steps: Who is affected: list everyone touched by each option and how seriously
What if everyone: imagine all people in a similar situation made this choice; would the world be better or worse?
Explain it: could you explain your choice, calmly and honestly, to someone whose judgement you respect, or to a newspaper reader?
Decide and own it: choose, accept the cost, and learn from what happens
scenarioSetup: Ruth finds a wallet with 15,000 naira and an ID card in the school corridor. Her friend says, 'Keep it, whoever lost it is careless.' Ruth's family has struggled to pay school fees this term.
scenarioWrong: Ruth keeps the money, then feels anxious for weeks every time she sees the owner, a junior student, asking about it.
scenarioBetter: Who is affected: the junior student, her family, her own conscience, the school community
What if everyone: if everyone kept found money, no one could trust others
Explain it: she knows she would be ashamed to tell her teacher she kept it
Decide: she hands the wallet to the office and later receives a small reward and a thank-you from the student's parent.
mistakes: Mistake: using 'everyone does it' as a justification. Fix: Popularity does not make something right.
Mistake: hiding behind rules. Fix: Understand why a rule exists and when it fails.
Mistake: thinking ethics is for important people. Fix: Practise in small daily choices.
lab: (5 min) Read a dilemma card and write your first instinct
(10 min) Discuss in groups using the three tests; each person speaks before debate
(10 min) Prepare and present your group's reasoning, not just the answer
(5 min) Note whether anyone changed their view and why
reflect: What ethical line would I never cross, and why?
When did the easy choice and the right choice differ for me?
Whose opinion helps me reason well?
takeaways: Test choices as if everyone did the same
Courage means keeping standards when it costs something
challenge: Write about a real ethical choice you faced or are facing. Apply the Three Ethics Tests and note what you decided and why. Add your reflection to your portfolio and discuss it with a trusted adult.

o: A choice between two obviously different options
A situation where values or goods conflict and there is no easy answer

check.q: The question 'What if everyone made this choice?' tests:
o: Whether it would be good as a general rule

check.q: Why do we discuss dilemmas in groups?
o: To hear other perspectives and sharpen our reasoning

summary: Plan and deliver a project with clear scope, tasks, timeline, risks and review points.
goals: Define the scope and success measure of a project in one paragraph
Break work into tasks with owners and deadlines
Identify two risks and plan to handle them
idea: A project is a temporary effort with a clear goal, a deadline and limited resources. From organising a school fair to launching a small business, projects succeed when someone plans them, tracks progress and adjusts. Planning is not paperwork; it is thinking ahead so that problems appear on paper rather than on the day.

Four ideas keep projects on track: scope (what is in and what is out), tasks and owners (who does what by when), risks (what could go wrong and what we will do) and review (regular check-ins). The MoSCoW method helps prioritise: Must have, Should have, Could have, Will not have this time.
oneLine: Scope it, break it into tasks with owners and dates, plan for risks and review regularly.
steps: Scope: write the goal, the deliverable, the deadline and what is out of scope; sort features using MoSCoW
Tasks: list every task, assign an owner and a due date, and order them on a simple timeline
Risks: list the top two or three risks, rate them, and write a backup, such as 'If the venue cancels, we use the school hall'
Review: hold a 10-minute check-in each week to update progress and fix blockers
scenarioSetup: A student club promises to hold a career day in three weeks. They discuss ideas excitedly but do not write anything down.
scenarioWrong: Nobody books speakers until week 2, the hall is double-booked and the event is cancelled the day before.
scenarioBetter: Scope: a two-hour career day with three speakers, 100 students, on the 20th; out of scope: food
Tasks: Ada books the hall by Monday; Tunde invites speakers by Wednesday; Zainab prepares the programme by Friday
Risks: speaker drops out, so keep two backups; hall clash, so book a second room
Review: short Friday check-ins to update a shared task list.
mistakes: Mistake: making plans that no one owns. Fix: Give every task a name and a date.
Mistake: adding more and more features. Fix: Protect the Musts and say no to extras.
Mistake: planning no slack. Fix: Add a buffer for delays.
lab: (5 min) Choose a mini-project, such as a class quiz or charity drive
(10 min) Write the scope and apply MoSCoW
(10 min) Create a task list with owners and dates
(5 min) Identify two risks and backups
reflect: Which project of mine went wrong, and what plan could have saved it?
Am I better at starting or finishing?
What project would I love to lead this year?
takeaways: Risks are easier to handle when planned
challenge: Plan a small real project (a family event, club activity or fundraiser) using the Scope, Tasks, Risks, Review method and carry it out. Record what changed from your plan and add your plan and results to your portfolio.

o: What is in and out of the project
So problems have a backup plan before they happen

summary: Learn leadership styles and adapt your approach to the person and the situation.
goals: Describe four leadership styles: directing, coaching, supporting and delegating
Match a style to a team member's skill and motivation
Identify your default style and one style to practise
idea: There is no single best way to lead. Situational leadership, developed by Paul Hersey and Ken Blanchard, suggests that the best style depends on the person and the task. A beginner who is eager needs clear direction; an experienced but discouraged person needs support; a skilled, confident person needs freedom.

Many young leaders have one default, such as bossing everyone or avoiding any conflict. Effective leaders learn to flex. They diagnose how skilled and motivated each person is for this particular task and choose the right balance of direction and support.
oneLine: Match your leadership style to the person's skill and motivation for the task.
methodName: Four Styles: Direct, Coach, Support, Delegate
steps: Direct: for low skill, high enthusiasm, give clear instructions, show how and check often
Coach: for some skill, lower confidence, explain why, ask questions and give encouragement
Support: for high skill, variable confidence, listen, encourage and let them decide how
Delegate: for high skill and high confidence, agree the goal and step back, offering help if asked
scenarioSetup: Ope leads a school radio team: Kayode is brand new, Sade is talented but upset after criticism, and Ife has produced the show for two years.
scenarioWrong: Ope gives everyone the same long instructions and is quick to correct. Kayode gets confused, Sade withdraws, and Ife feels micromanaged.
scenarioBetter: Kayode: direct, with a step-by-step checklist and a buddy
Sade: support, with praise for specific strengths and a chance to decide her segment
Ife: delegate, with the goal 'produce the Friday show' and a check-in only if needed
Ope reviews each person's progress weekly and adjusts.
mistakes: Mistake: using one style for everyone. Fix: Diagnose each person and task.
Mistake: delegating to a beginner without support. Fix: Teach first, then delegate.
Mistake: micromanaging experts. Fix: Agree outcomes and trust them.
lab: (5 min) Read four short team member profiles and match each to a style
(10 min) Role-play giving the same instruction in two different styles
(10 min) Complete a quick self-assessment of your default style
(5 min) Choose one style to practise this week
reflect: Which leaders helped me grow, and what style did they use?
What is my default style and what is its risk?
Who needs a different style from me?
takeaways: Skill and motivation guide the choice
Flexible leaders get more from teams
challenge: Choose a real group (class, sport, family project) and practise at least two styles with different people, then reflect on the results. Record your reflection and add it to your portfolio.

check.q: Which style best fits someone new but enthusiastic?

o: Best style depends on the person and task

summary: Lead a team with a shared vision, clear roles, healthy meetings and psychological safety.
goals: Write a one-sentence team vision that people can repeat
Run a 15-minute meeting with an agenda, decisions and actions
Create psychological safety so that people can speak up without fear
idea: Leading a team means helping a group of different people work toward the same goal. Research by Google on its own teams found that the most important factor in high-performing teams was psychological safety, a shared belief that it is safe to ask questions, admit mistakes and share ideas without being humiliated.

Leaders build this with simple habits: a clear vision, defined roles, short and purposeful meetings, fair recognition and a calm response to mistakes. How a leader reacts the first time someone admits an error decides whether anyone ever admits one again.
oneLine: Give your team a clear vision, regular rhythm, fair recognition and a safe place to speak up.
steps: Vision: write one sentence the whole team can repeat, 'We will give every Year 7 student a friend by Friday.'
Roles: make sure everyone knows their part and who decides what
Rhythm: hold a short, regular meeting with an agenda, decisions recorded and next steps assigned
Recognition: thank people specifically and respond to mistakes with 'What can we learn?' instead of blame
scenarioSetup: Amina leads the science club. In meetings she speaks most of the time, rolls her eyes at weak ideas and becomes angry when a member forgets the equipment.
scenarioWrong: Members stop sharing ideas, and two quit. Amina thinks, 'They are not committed.'
scenarioBetter: Vision: 'Every member runs one experiment this term.'
Roles: a rota for equipment, with a backup
Rhythm: a 15-minute weekly meeting with a written agenda, everyone speaks once before anyone speaks twice
Recognition: 'Thanks, Yusuf, for the great demo.' When equipment is missing: 'What can we change in the rota?'
mistakes: Mistake: dominating the talk. Fix: Ask quiet members first.
Mistake: criticising in public. Fix: Give corrections privately and praise publicly.
Mistake: long meetings without decisions. Fix: Use an agenda and finish with actions.
lab: (5 min) Write a vision sentence for a real group you lead or could lead
(10 min) Draft a 15-minute meeting agenda
(10 min) Run a mock meeting where the leader practises inviting quiet voices
(5 min) Discuss how mistakes were handled
reflect: How do I react when someone admits a mistake?
Do people feel safe speaking up around me?
What recognition would motivate my team?
takeaways: Psychological safety is the foundation of strong teams
Vision, roles and rhythm keep a team aligned
challenge: Lead a short meeting in a real group this week using an agenda, invite every voice and record decisions and actions. Collect feedback afterwards and add the agenda and feedback to your portfolio.

o: A belief that you can speak up or admit mistakes without being humiliated

check.q: Which makes a meeting more effective?
o: A clear agenda, decisions and action list

check.q: A member admits a mistake. The best leader response is:
o: Ask what can be learned and how to fix it

summary: Behave responsibly, respectfully and safely online and protect your digital footprint.
goals: Explain what a digital footprint is and why it lasts
Apply the THINK test before posting: True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind
Respond to online unkindness by documenting, blocking, reporting and telling a trusted adult
idea: Digital citizenship means using technology responsibly, respectfully and safely. Everything you post, like, comment on or search leaves a trail called your digital footprint. Universities and employers often search for candidates online, and screenshots can travel further than you ever intended.

The internet also feels anonymous, which can make people cruel or careless. Remember that there is a real person behind every screen. Respect, privacy and kindness online matter as much as they do in the school yard, and the consequences can be bigger because content spreads and lasts.
oneLine: Treat your online life like a permanent, public record: think before you post and be kind.
steps: True: is it accurate, or am I sharing a rumour?
Helpful and Inspiring: does it help or encourage someone?
Necessary: does it need to be said, and does it need to be said publicly?
Kind: would I say this to their face, and would I be comfortable if my parents or a future employer read it?
scenarioSetup: After a football loss, Tayo posts a rude meme mocking a teammate's mistake. It gets many likes. The teammate stops coming to practice.
scenarioWrong: Tayo says, 'It was only a joke,' but the post is screenshotted, shared and later seen by the coach and some parents.
scenarioBetter: He pauses and applies THINK: not kind, not necessary
He deletes the post, apologises privately and shares the team's supportive message instead
If he receives mean messages about his own mistakes, he screenshots, blocks, reports and tells his coach.
mistakes: Mistake: believing deleted means gone. Fix: Assume anything posted can be saved.
Mistake: sharing private details such as your school, address or location. Fix: Keep personal information private.
Mistake: joining pile-ons. Fix: Do not like or share unkind posts; support the target privately.
lab: (5 min) Search your name (or a made-up student name) and discuss what a stranger would learn
(10 min) Review five sample posts and apply the THINK test
(10 min) Role-play responding to an unkind comment and to a friend who posted something harmful
(5 min) Write three personal rules for your online life
reflect: What would I be embarrassed for my future boss to see?
Do I behave differently online than offline, and why?
Who would I tell if I felt unsafe online?
takeaways: Report and support when you see harm
challenge: Audit your own accounts: remove or fix any posts you would not want a future employer to see, tighten privacy settings, and write your three online rules. Add the rules (not any private details) to your portfolio.

o: The trail of data and posts you leave online
Does it need to be said, and publicly?

check.q: If someone bullies you online, which sequence is best?
o: Screenshot, block, report and tell a trusted adult

summary: Use digital tools effectively: search smartly, judge information, organise work and create and share.
goals: Search with precise keywords and operators to find reliable information
Evaluate a website using the CRAAP checklist: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose
Use basic documents, spreadsheets and cloud storage to organise and share work
idea: Digital literacy is the ability to find, evaluate, create and communicate information using technology. Being able to scroll quickly is not the same as being digitally literate. Many young people are confident users but weak at judging reliability or using tools for productivity.

Searching well is a skill: specific keywords, quotation marks for exact phrases and the right site types (such as .edu or .gov) give better results. Evaluating what you find matters even more, because anyone can publish anything. Finally, productive tools such as documents, spreadsheets and cloud folders help you organise work, collaborate and never lose a project.
oneLine: Find it well, check it carefully, create something useful and share it responsibly.
steps: Find: use specific keywords, quote exact phrases and try more than one search engine or source
Evaluate: check Currency (how recent), Relevance, Authority (who wrote it), Accuracy (can it be verified) and Purpose (to inform, sell or persuade)
Create: turn information into something useful: notes, a spreadsheet, a chart, a short presentation, in your own words
Share: store files with clear names, use cloud folders and share links with the right permissions
scenarioSetup: Halima needs facts on renewable energy in Nigeria for a presentation. She types 'energy' into a search engine and copies the first result.
scenarioWrong: The result is an old blog post from a seller of solar panels. She presents outdated numbers and loses marks.
scenarioBetter: Find: 'renewable energy Nigeria 2025 statistics' with quotation marks around 'renewable energy'
Evaluate: choose a government agency and a university report, checking dates and authors
Create: record figures in a spreadsheet and make one chart in her own words
Share: save to a cloud folder named 'Energy Presentation', set to 'view only' for classmates.
mistakes: Mistake: trusting the first result. Fix: Compare at least two reliable sources.
Mistake: copying and pasting. Fix: Summarise in your own words and cite sources.
Mistake: poor file names ('final final 2'). Fix: Use clear names with dates.
lab: (5 min) Practise three searches with different keywords on the same question
(10 min) Evaluate two web pages using CRAAP
(10 min) Create a simple spreadsheet with three columns and make a chart
(5 min) Save, name and share the file with view permissions
reflect: Where do I usually get information, and how reliable is it?
Which digital tool could save me the most time?
How do I organise my files, and what could improve?
challenge: Use Find, Evaluate, Create and Share to produce a one-page fact sheet on a topic you care about, with at least three reliable sources noted. Add the fact sheet to your portfolio.

check.q: What does the 'A' in CRAAP stand for?
Which search is likely to give better results?
Why compare more than one source?
o: To check accuracy and avoid bias
It is a rule only for teachers

summary: Use AI as a smart assistant while staying honest, accurate and in charge of your own thinking.
goals: Explain in simple terms what generative AI can and cannot do
Write a clear prompt using Role, Task, Context, Format
Verify AI output, protect private data and state when you used AI
idea: Generative AI tools can write, summarise, translate and brainstorm, but they predict plausible words; they do not 'know' things and can state falsehoods confidently, a problem often called hallucination. They can also reflect biases in the data they learned from. That makes them powerful assistants and risky authorities.

Responsible use has three habits: be clear about what you want, always verify important facts, and be honest about when you used AI, following your school's rules. Never paste private information such as passwords, ID numbers or other people's personal details into a tool. The aim is to think better with AI, not to stop thinking.
oneLine: Use AI as a co-pilot: prompt clearly, verify everything important, protect privacy and be honest about its use.
steps: Prompt: give a Role ('act as a tutor'), Task ('explain photosynthesis'), Context ('for a 14-year-old') and Format ('in five bullet points')
Verify: check key facts, numbers and quotes in reliable sources; ask the tool for sources and then confirm they exist
Protect: never share passwords, personal data or private images, and be careful with uploaded files
Disclose: say when and how you used AI, and do your own thinking; follow school and exam rules
scenarioSetup: Nkechi is told to write a short report on the history of the Nigerian railway. She asks an AI to 'write it' and submits what it gives her.
scenarioWrong: The report contains two invented dates and a made-up quotation. Her teacher notices and gives a zero for dishonesty.
scenarioBetter: Prompt: 'Act as a history tutor. Give me an outline of the main periods of Nigerian railway development for a 15-year-old, as five bullet points.'
Verify: she checks each date in a library book and a reputable encyclopaedia
Protect: she does not include personal details

summary: Keep yourself and your accounts safe from scams, phishing and weak security.
goals: Recognise phishing and common online scams in messages and links
Create a strong password and turn on two-factor authentication
Apply Stop, Look, Verify before clicking, paying or sharing
idea: Cyber criminals prefer to trick people rather than hack machines, because it is easier. Phishing messages pretend to be from your bank, a prize organiser or a friend, and push you to click quickly, often with urgency such as 'Your account will be closed in 24 hours'.

You can reduce most risks with a few habits: strong, unique passwords (ideally a long phrase), a password manager if possible, two-factor authentication, updated devices and careful checking of links and senders. If something feels too good to be true or too urgent, it usually is.
oneLine: Slow down, check the sender and link, use strong passwords and two-factor protection.
steps: Stop: pause when a message creates urgency, fear or excitement; scammers want you to act before thinking
Look: check the sender's address, spelling, odd links and requests for passwords, codes, PINs or payment
Verify: contact the organisation through its official website or number, not through the message; ask an adult
Protect: use a long unique password phrase, turn on two-factor authentication and report or delete the message
scenarioSetup: Ikenna gets an SMS: 'Congratulations! You won 500,000 naira. Click here and enter your bank details to claim.' He is excited because his family could use the money.
scenarioWrong: He clicks, enters his details and later finds that money is missing from his parent's account.
scenarioBetter: Stop: he notices the urgency and that he never entered a contest
Look: the link is not an official bank domain, and it asks for his PIN
Verify: he tells his parents and calls the bank using the number on the card
Protect: they delete and report the message and change a password that was reused.
mistakes: Mistake: reusing one password everywhere. Fix: Use unique passwords or a password manager.
Mistake: sharing one-time codes. Fix: Never give codes to anyone, even someone claiming to be the bank.
Mistake: clicking to 'see what happens'. Fix: Verify first.

takeaways: Strong passwords and 2FA block most attacks

summary: Build a personal brand that is honest, consistent and backed by proof of your skills.
goals: Explain personal branding as the reputation you build, not self-promotion
Write a brand statement using Values, Strengths, Story, Proof
Create a short, consistent online profile or bio
idea: Your personal brand is what people say about you when you are not in the room. You already have one; the question is whether you shape it on purpose. A strong brand is honest: it is built from your real values and strengths, shown consistently, and backed by proof such as projects, results and references.

In the digital world, people will often meet your brand online first. Consistency matters: your tone, photo and message across platforms should tell the same story. Authenticity matters more: a brand built on exaggeration collapses at the first meeting.
oneLine: Know your values and strengths, tell your story and show proof, consistently and honestly.
steps: Values: choose two or three values you want to be known for (from Week 5)
Strengths: pick two or three strengths with evidence (from Week 3)
Story: write a short story or line that shows these in action (from Week 16)
Proof: gather evidence, such as a project, certificate, testimonial or portfolio piece, and write a short bio such as 'I am a curious student who uses coding to solve community problems.'
scenarioSetup: Joy is applying for a youth leadership programme. Her social media is full of jokes at others' expense, and her bio says, 'No filter, no regrets.'
scenarioWrong: The selectors see an unfocused and sometimes unkind profile and doubt her maturity.
scenarioBetter: Values: kindness and curiosity
Strengths: organising and public speaking
Story: she started a reading club for neighbourhood children
Proof: photos of the club, a letter from a teacher and a short bio. She clears out harmful posts and updates her bio: 'Joy, 15. Reading-club founder. Curious about people and ideas.'
mistakes: Mistake: pretending to be someone else. Fix: Be your best self, not a fake self.
Mistake: inconsistent messages across platforms. Fix: Align photo, tone and bio.
Mistake: no proof. Fix: Show projects and results.

reflect: What would my friends, teachers and family say is my brand?

takeaways: Your brand is your reputation, so shape it
